# Bryn by Civic — full documentation

> Bryn is the Signal-Based GTM agent for Growth teams. Bryn watches anonymous and known product, web, and intent signals, names the pattern, and runs the Play you approved, with the audit log attached. This file holds the full text of the Bryn docs at https://docs.civic.com/bryn. For a short index, see https://docs.civic.com/llms.txt.

---

# Start here

## Bryn

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn

**Bryn is the Signal-Based GTM agent for Growth teams.**

Bryn watches anonymous and known product, web, and intent signals, names the
pattern, and runs the Play you approved, with the audit log attached.

In practice: Bryn tells you which companies are on your website, understands
what they are doing there, and acts on it inside rules you set. A good-fit
account keeps returning to your pricing page, and your sales channel hears
about it in Slack with the evidence attached. The same identification can
update your CRM or personalize the page the visitor is looking at.

*From anonymous visit to action: how a page view becomes a Slack alert. The
full walkthrough is on [How Bryn works](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/how-bryn-works).*

### Where to start

**[Get started](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/getting-started)**
Your first identified visitor in Slack in about 30 minutes.

**[How Bryn works](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/how-bryn-works)**
The whole loop in one picture: pixel, identity, signals, score, Plays.

**[Personalization recipes](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes)**
Copy-paste snippets that personalize your site for identified visitors.

**[Advanced](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api-overview)**
The Control Plane API, request signing, and the MCP server.

## Get started with Bryn

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/getting-started

Bryn's onboarding is a six-step wizard. Most teams finish it in about 30
minutes, and at the end Bryn is live: watching your traffic, naming signals,
and alerting your Slack channel when a qualified account shows up.

### Before you start

Check that you have:

- A work email address to sign up with. Your workspace is created from it.
- Edit access to your website's `<head>` or to your tag manager, or a
  developer you can hand one snippet to.
- A Slack workspace where you can approve app installs.

### The six steps

**Create your workspace**

Sign up with your work email. Bryn creates a workspace for your company
and drops you into the wizard.

**You'll know it worked when** the wizard greets you inside your new
workspace.

**Install the pixel**

One snippet, site-wide. Paste it into your site's `<head>`, add it
through Google Tag Manager, or send the instructions to your developer.
Nothing else in Bryn works without this step. Full walkthrough:
[Install the pixel](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/pixel).

**You'll know it worked when** your own visit shows up in **Activity**
in the Bryn dashboard.

**Confirm your ideal customer**

Bryn proposes an Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) from your website and
industry. Review it and adjust what's off. You are editing a draft, not
writing from scratch. Details: [Define your ICP & scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring).

**You'll know it worked when** the wizard shows your ICP as confirmed.

**Map your signals**

Tell Bryn which of your events matter and what to call them, using the
sentence builder: when this event happens, raise this signal. Details:
[Map your signals](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).

**You'll know it worked when** a test event shows up as a named signal
on an account.

**Connect Slack**

Authorize the Slack app and pick a channel. Bryn posts a test message on
connect, so verification is built in. Details:
[Connect Slack & other outputs](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/outputs).

**You'll know it worked when** you see "Test message delivered" and the
message is in your channel.

**Review and turn on your Plays**

Bryn ships with pre-built Plays: automated workflows that act on
qualified accounts. Review the ones proposed for you and switch your
first one on. Nothing runs until you do. Details:
[Turn on Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays).

**You'll know it worked when** the Play shows as active, and the first
matching account produces a Slack alert.

### What happens next

Bryn runs on its own from here. On day two, look at:

- **Accounts**: companies from your traffic, scored and ranked by buying
  intent.
- **Activity**: every Play run and what triggered it.
- Your Slack channel: alerts arrive as matching accounts show up.

A good second win is on-page personalization: the pixel you already
installed can also tailor your site for identified visitors. Start with the
[Personalization recipes](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes).

## How Bryn works

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/how-bryn-works

Bryn watches. You decide the Play. Bryn runs it.

This page is the mental model behind that sentence: five stages, one
diagram, and a glossary for when you meet the API's names for things.

### Identification

The [pixel](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/pixel) reports each visit. Bryn works with identity
providers to resolve the visitor's company, and where possible the person.
Honesty about the shape of this: **company-level identification is the
common case**. Knowing the person is the bonus, not the default, which is
why everything downstream works at the account level first.

Identities from other sources stitch to the same records: a PostHog event
or a webhook event carrying a known email joins the same account the pixel
saw.

**Privacy**: identification targets business traffic. Erasure requests
propagate through Bryn's stores, suppression is enforced before anything
is served to a page, and the pixel's origin allowlist rejects events from
domains you have not approved.

### Signals

Bryn turns raw events into named signals using
[the mapping you define](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping). A signal is a judgement
with a name: `pricing_page_viewed`, `demo_abandonment`, `trial_wobble`.
Signals, not raw events, are what scoring, Plays, and personalization
consume.

### Scoring

Every account gets a transparent score:
[Fit, Intent, Timing, and their Composite](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring). Scores
rank the **Accounts** list and gate Play triggers. For any account you can
see exactly which signals produced the number. Scores reach your website
only when you turn them on in the pixel's
[returned fields](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes#choose-what-comes-back).

### Plays

When a trigger matches, the [Play](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays) runs: alert, draft,
route, CRM update. Governance is built into the runtime, not bolted on:
holds for review, a one-click kill switch, cooldowns, and an append-only
audit log that records every signal, score, match, and execution.

### The return leg

The same pixel that reports visits receives a personalization payload,
usually in well under a second. Your page reacts with a few lines of
JavaScript or with declarative attributes and no JavaScript at all. The
[Personalization recipes](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes) are the copy-paste
starting point.

### Glossary

The docs use customer words; the API and payloads use the engine's nouns.
The mapping:

| Docs say | The API says | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| account (or company) | `entity` | The company Bryn identified and scores |
| person | `individual` | The specific human, when known |
| signal | `signal` | A named interpretation of behaviour |
| Play | `play` | Trigger, conditions, and actions, run by Bryn |
| pixel | `pixel` | The one script on your site, both directions |
| Bryn dashboard | Control Plane | The web app at your workspace URL |

Programmatic access to all of it: the
[API overview](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api-overview).

---

# Set up Bryn

## Install the pixel

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/pixel

The pixel is how Bryn sees your website traffic. Without it, Bryn cannot
identify anyone. Install it **site-wide**: identification improves with
coverage, and a single-page install misses most of the visitors Bryn could
have named for you.

One snippet does two jobs: it reports visits to Bryn, and it receives the
payload that lets your site personalize for identified visitors.

### Before you start

- Your **pixel ref**: shown on the Pixel step of onboarding, and in your
  Bryn dashboard.
- Edit access to your site's `<head>` template or your tag manager. No
  access? Skip to [hand it off](#hand-it-off).

### Install it

Pick your platform:

**Google Tag Manager**

No code changes on your site. Bryn ships an official GTM tag template.

**Import the template**

In GTM, go to **Templates**, then **Search Gallery**, and search for
**Bryn Pixel** (published from the
[civicteam/bryn-google-tag-manager](https://github.com/civicteam/bryn-google-tag-manager)
repository).

**Create the tag**

Add a new tag using the template and paste your pixel ref into the
**Pixel ref** field. Use the copy button in the Bryn dashboard so no
stray characters come along.

**Trigger on all pages**

Set the trigger to **All Pages**, then publish the container.

**Any website (HTML)**

Paste this into your site-wide `<head>` template, replacing
`YOUR_PIXEL_REF` with your pixel ref:

```html
<script>
(function () {
  window.__brynPixel = { ref: "YOUR_PIXEL_REF" };
  var s = document.createElement('script');
  s.src = "https://bryn.civic.com/pixel/pixel.js";
  s.async = true;
  s.setAttribute('data-bryn-pixel-ref', "YOUR_PIXEL_REF");
  document.head.appendChild(s);
})();
</script>
```

Put it in the shared layout or header template, not on a single page,
so every page reports.

**Options.** Two attributes on the script tag tune the pixel:
`data-bryn-personalize="off"` reports visits and skips the
personalization leg entirely (no polling, no `bryn:updated` or
`bryn:personalize`, no PostHog write), and
`data-bryn-debug="true"` logs each delivery step to `console.debug`.
Tag managers set the same options on the config global instead:

```js
window.__brynPixel = { ref: "YOUR_PIXEL_REF", personalize: false, debug: true };
```

`__brynPixel` also accepts `endpoint` for a custom collection origin. A
CSP `nonce` on your script tag is forwarded to the bundle it loads, so
strict-CSP sites work with a nonced tag. The pixel initializes once per
pixel ref: a tag-manager install alongside a leftover manual snippet
reports each visit once.

**Webflow**

In Webflow, go to **Site settings**, then **Custom code**, and paste the
snippet from the HTML tab into **Head code**. Publish the site.

**WordPress**

Add the snippet from the HTML tab to your theme's site-wide header:
either through your theme's "header scripts" setting or with a
header/footer snippet plugin. Avoid pasting it into a single post or
page.

### Hand it off

Not the person who edits the website? Send your developer this page link
and your pixel ref, with one line: "Please add this script tag to our
site-wide head template so it loads on every page." The
[verification step](#verify-its-working) below tells them (and you) that
it worked.

### Verify it's working

Open your site in a normal browser tab, click around, then check
**Activity** in the Bryn dashboard. Your visit arrives within moments of
the pixel going live.

You may not see yourself **identified**, and that is normal. The pixel
reports every visit, but Bryn only resolves identities for business
traffic it can match. Seeing the visit in Activity means the pixel works,
even while your own visit stays anonymous.

#### Check it in the browser

Open the console on any page with the pixel and read
`window.__brynPixelDiagnostics`:

```js
{
  publish: { state: "sent-beacon" },   // sent-beacon | sent-fetch | failed | unavailable
  serve: {
    lastOutcome: "ok",
    consecutiveFailures: 0,
    loopState: "polling",              // polling | paused | stopped
    stopReason: undefined              // set when stopped, e.g. "suppressed", "collection-only", "idle-ceiling"
  }
}
```

`publish.state` confirms the visit left the browser. `serve` describes the
personalization leg: it polls for the payload, pauses while the tab is in
the background, and stops 30 minutes after the last payload change once the
visitor is resolved. Every change fires a `bryn:delivery` event with the same
snapshot in `event.detail`, so a status chip or a QA script can follow it
live.

### For your IT and security team

What the pixel does, in one screen:

- **Sends**: five fields on each page view: `url`, `referrer`, `ts`, plus
  `firstUrl` and `firstReferrer`, the first page and referrer of the browser
  session. The pixel keeps that first touch in `sessionStorage` under
  `bryn:first-touch`, so it clears when the tab closes.
- **Returns**: only the visitor fields your workspace chooses under
  **Integrations**, then **Pixel**, then **Returned fields**. Bryn filters
  them on its servers, so a field that's turned off never reaches the
  browser. Anything returned, scores included, is readable by the visitor
  in their own browser.
- **Writes to your PostHog**: when PostHog runs on your page and **PostHog
  sync** is on (the default), the pixel writes the returned fields onto
  the visitor's PostHog person, under a single `bryn` property. It never
  changes who PostHog thinks the visitor is. Turn it off under
  **Integrations**, then **Pixel**, then **Setup**.
- **Never touches**: form fields, keystrokes, cookies from other tools.
- **Origin allowlist**: Bryn only accepts events from domains on your
  workspace's allowlist, and rejects everything else.
- **Personalization writes are inert by default**: the return leg only sets
  text content and the standard `hidden` attribute on elements you mark,
  which keeps it XSS-safe. If you never add markers, it changes nothing.
  `data-bryn-personalize="off"` turns the return leg off altogether.
- **Polite polling**: the return leg pauses in background tabs and stops
  after 30 idle minutes once the visitor is resolved.
- **CSP**: a `nonce` on the script tag carries through to the loaded bundle.
- **Erasure**: deletion requests propagate through Bryn's stores. See
  [How Bryn works](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/how-bryn-works) for the identification model.

### Going further

- React to identified visitors on the page:
  [Personalization recipes](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes)
- Choose which fields, enrichment and scores the pixel returns:
  [Choose what comes back](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes#choose-what-comes-back)
- Name the behaviour the pixel observes: [Map your signals](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping)
- Send events from your backend too:
  [Server-side events & signing](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signing)
- Manage the origin allowlist programmatically: Pixel Origins in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api)

## Map your signals

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping

Raw events are noise. Signals are the vocabulary everything else in Bryn
speaks: scoring reads signals, Plays trigger on signals, and on-page
personalization reacts to signals. An event you never map does nothing.

### Where events come from

- **The pixel**: page views arrive automatically once the pixel is
  [installed](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/pixel).
- **Product analytics**: events from your PostHog project, if connected.
- **Your own systems**: anything you send to the custom webhook. See
  [Server-side events & signing](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signing).

You map; Bryn listens. Mapping lives in **Configuration**, then
**Signal Mapping**, in the Bryn dashboard.

### Map a signal

The sentence builder reads the way you would say it out loud: **when**
this event happens, **raise** this signal.

**Pick the event**

Choose from events Bryn has already observed, or use
**An event I haven't seen yet** to map one before it first arrives.

**Narrow it if needed**

Add a **where** clause to match on an event property, for example
where `path` contains `/pricing`. Skip this when the event name alone
says enough.

**Name the signal**

Pick an existing signal or **Create new signal**. Names normalize to
snake_case, like `demo_abandonment` or `pricing_page_viewed`.

**Save the rule**

Click **Save rule**. The rule reads back as a sentence: when
`demo_abandoned` happens, raise `demo_abandonment`.

**Worked example**: your demo form fires a `demo_abandoned` event when
someone starts but does not finish. Map it to a `demo_abandonment` signal,
and it becomes usable everywhere at once: a Play can alert sales, and the
[demo follow-up recipe](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes) can greet the visitor when
they return.

### Naming signals well

Signal names become the words in your Plays and your page snippets, so
pick names you want to read in an alert:

- Name the meaning, not the mechanism: `pricing_interest`, not
  `clicked_div_47`.
- Keep them stable. Renaming a signal later breaks the Plays and snippets
  that reference it.
- Short is fine. Two or three words in snake_case is the norm.

### Verify it's working

Trigger the event yourself (visit the page, abandon the test form), then
open the matching account and look for the signal on it. New signals also
show up as the trigger in **Activity** the first time a Play fires on
them.

### Going further

- Some signals work without any mapping: Bryn derives defaults, like
  repeat visits, from pixel traffic on its own.
- See what's arriving before you map it: Bryn samples observed events so
  you map real names, not guesses.
- Bulk edits and automation: Signal Mapping in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api).

## Define your ICP and scoring

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring

The score decides which accounts Bryn bothers you about. A wrong Ideal
Customer Profile (ICP) means alerts about companies you would never sell
to; a good one means your Slack channel stays worth reading.

### Confirm your ICP

During onboarding, Bryn proposes an ICP from your website and industry.
You review and adjust rather than write from scratch. After onboarding it
lives in **Configuration**, then **ICP**, in the Bryn dashboard.

The ICP describes the company you sell to: industry, size, region, stage.
Bryn compares every identified account against it, so edit the fields that
are wrong and leave the rest alone.

**You'll know it worked when** the wizard shows your ICP as confirmed, and
the **Accounts** list starts ranking companies you recognize as good fits
near the top.

### How scoring works

Bryn scores every account on three axes and blends them:

| Axis | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Fit** | Does this company look like your ICP? |
| **Intent** | Is it behaving like a buyer: pricing visits, repeat sessions, high-intent signals? |
| **Timing** | Is it happening now, or was that last month? |
| **Composite** | The blend of the three. Plays usually trigger on this one. |

Scores are explainable: for any account you can see which signals and
attributes produced the number. Scores reach your website only if you
turn them on: the pixel can return the fit grade and each score, so your
pages can react to them. Pick them in the pixel's
[returned fields](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/frontend-recipes#choose-what-comes-back). A
visitor can read anything the pixel returns, their own scores included.

### Your value proposition

One short paragraph, in your voice, describing what you offer and to whom.
Bryn uses it when drafting outreach text, so write it the way you would
want a prospect to read it. It lives alongside the ICP in Configuration.

### Leave the defaults alone (at first)

The default scoring weights are good. Change them after you have watched a
week of real traffic, not before. When you do review, look for two things:

- Accounts scored high that your team would ignore. Usually a Fit problem:
  tighten the ICP.
- Accounts your team chased that Bryn scored low. Usually an Intent
  problem: check whether the behaviour that convinced your team is mapped
  as a [signal](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping) at all.

Weights live in **Configuration**, then **Scoring Weights**.

### Going further

- Programmatic access: Icp, Scoring Config, and Value Proposition in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api).

## Connect Slack and other outputs

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/outputs

Bryn's work is invisible until it lands somewhere your team already looks.
Outputs are the destinations Plays deliver to. Slack is the fastest first
output; CRM and webhooks follow once alerts are flowing.

Outputs live under **Integrations** in the Bryn dashboard, and the
onboarding wizard walks you through the first one.

### Connect Slack

**Authorize**

Click **Connect to Slack** and approve the app in your Slack
workspace.

**Pick a channel**

A dedicated channel like `#intent` keeps alerts easy to follow and
easy to mute-proof. You can add more connections to other channels
later.

**Watch the test message arrive**

Bryn verifies the connection by posting a test message as soon as you
connect. No extra step.

**You'll know it worked when** the dashboard shows "Test message delivered
to #your-channel" and the message is sitting in Slack. If it failed, fix
the channel choice and click **Retry test**; a **Re-test** button stays
available on healthy connections too.

### Other destinations

- **CRM**: Bryn writes additively. It fills empty fields and adds notes and
  flags; it never overwrites data your team entered. Conflicting values go
  to a review queue instead of clobbering the record.
- **Outbound webhooks**: receive structured records in your own systems.
  The request contract and verification steps are in
  [Server-side events & signing](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signing).

### Keeping it quiet

Alerts you mute are worse than no alerts, so Bryn rate-limits itself:

- **Cooldowns** stop the same Play re-firing on the same account for a
  configurable window (a week by default).
- **Workspace caps** keep total alert volume bounded even during a traffic
  spike.

If a channel feels noisy, tighten the Play's trigger or your
[Ideal Customer Profile (ICP)](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring) rather than muting
the channel.

### Going further

- Manage connections programmatically: Outputs and Integrations in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api).

## Turn on Plays

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays

Identification without action is a dashboard you will stop checking. Plays
are how Bryn acts on what it sees: automated workflows that fire when an
account does something that matters, inside rules you set once.

### Anatomy of a Play

- **Trigger**: what the account did. Signals and score thresholds, like
  `pricing_page_viewed` plus a climbing intent score.
- **Conditions**: who it applies to. Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP),
  trial state, account attributes.
- **Actions**: what happens. Alert Slack, draft outreach, update the CRM.
  Outbound actions can hold for a human review first.

### The pre-built library

Bryn ships with Plays authored for the common moments. The first three are
on for new workspaces; the rest wait for you:

**Slack alert for active accounts**
A qualified account is active on your site right now; the channel hears
about it with the evidence attached.

**Outbound brief when intent climbs**
Intent keeps rising on a good-fit account, so Bryn drafts the outreach
note and holds it for a salesperson.

**Trial wobble assist for your AEs**
A trial goes quiet before day 14; the owner gets a heads-up and a
suggested rescue.

**ICP-match alert from website visitors**
A visitor resolves to a company matching your ICP; sales knows the same
day.

**Account review with a recommended next step**
Bryn assembles what an account did and recommends what to do about it.

**Follow up when a demo is left unfinished**
Someone starts a demo and bails; Bryn flags it so the thread does not
go cold.

### Enable your first Play

**Open Plays**

In the Bryn dashboard, go to **Plays**. Each Play shows its trigger and
what it will do.

**Review the rules**

Check the trigger and conditions read the way you want. The signals it
references come from [your mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).

**Switch it on**

Flip the toggle. A Play starts or stops right away, and nothing runs
while it is off.

**You'll know it worked when** the Play shows as active, and the first
matching account produces its action: watch **Activity** for the run and
your Slack channel for the alert.

### Stay in control

Autonomy inside bounds is the whole design. Every control is a feature you
can point your reviewers at:

- **Nothing sends without you.** Plays with outbound actions hold the run
  for review: the held run shows in **Activity** with an **Unhold** button,
  or an approval link in Slack.
- **The kill switch is a single click.** **Pause this Play** stops one;
  **Pause all Plays** stops everything at once, and resuming is just as
  fast.
- **Every action is on the record.** The **Audit log** captures every
  signal, score, match, and execution: your work record, and the same
  trail your CFO and DPO inherit.
- **Cooldowns** stop the same Play re-firing on the same account, a week
  by default.

### Going further

- Play management and run history: Plays and Play Executions in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api).

---

# Connectors

## Connectors

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors

A connector links Bryn to a tool your team already uses. Every connector
works in one or more of three modes, in the order data moves through Bryn:

- **Input**: the tool sends events into Bryn. Bryn turns them into
  [signals](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping) and stitches them to the same accounts
  and people the [pixel](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/pixel) sees.
- **Enrichment**: Bryn looks accounts and people up in the tool to fill in
  what it knows about them. Enrichment feeds [scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring)
  and gives Plays more to work with. It never delivers anything.
- **Output**: a [Play](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays) delivers to the tool: an alert in a
  chat channel, a contact in a CRM, a person enrolled in a sequence, a
  ticket, an email, or a webhook call.

You connect each one under **Integrations** in the Bryn dashboard. Each
connector's page covers what Bryn does with it in every mode it supports,
how to connect it, and where to find the vendor's own documentation.

### Available connectors

| Connector | Input | Enrichment | Output |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Amazon SES |  |  | ✓ |
| [Apify](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/apify) | ✓ | ✓ |  |
| [Apollo](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/apollo) |  | ✓ | ✓ |
| [Calendly](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/calendly) | ✓ |  |  |
| [Clay](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/clay) |  | ✓ |  |
| Discord |  |  | ✓ |
| Findymail | ✓ | ✓ |  |
| Firecrawl | ✓ | ✓ |  |
| HeyReach | ✓ |  | ✓ |
| HubSpot | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Instantly |  | ✓ | ✓ |
| Jira |  |  | ✓ |
| Linear |  |  | ✓ |
| Microsoft Teams |  |  | ✓ |
| MoltSets |  | ✓ |  |
| Outgoing webhook |  |  | ✓ |
| Pipedrive | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Postmark |  |  | ✓ |
| Resend |  |  | ✓ |
| Slack |  |  | ✓ |
| Tavily |  | ✓ |  |
| Zoho CRM | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

Connectors without a link are available in the Bryn dashboard today; their
pages here are on the way.

Enrichment here includes tools that also take deliveries: a CRM or
sequencing tool connected for output is also a place Bryn can look people
and accounts up.

### Going further

- Start with the fastest first output: [Connect Slack and other outputs](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/outputs).
- Send events from your own backend: [Server-side events and signing](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signing).
- Manage connections programmatically: Outputs and Integrations in the
  [API reference](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/api/bryn-control-plane-api).

## Amazon SES

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/amazon-ses

Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) is the AWS service for sending email from
your own domain. Bryn connects to SES as an **Output** connector: you give
Bryn an AWS access key, the region your sender lives in, a verified From
address, and a To address, and Bryn sends through your SES account rather
than its own.

SES supports one mode in Bryn: Output, for email.

### How Bryn integrates Amazon SES

The connection uses an AWS access key pair, not OAuth. You set it up under
[**Integrations**](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations) in the Bryn
dashboard, in a form with five fields:

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Access key ID** | The access key ID of an IAM user or role in the AWS account that owns your SES identities |
| **Secret access key** | The matching secret access key |
| **Region** | The AWS region where your sender identity is verified, for example `us-east-1` |
| **From address** | The address mail is sent from. It must be a verified identity in SES in that region |
| **To address** | The single address this connection delivers to, for example a team inbox |

Bryn stores the key pair as a secret and keeps the region, From address and
To address as ordinary settings. The Bryn dashboard lists the connection by
its From address, with the To address and region underneath.

Each connection is one route: one region, one From address, one To address.
The Bryn dashboard holds one Amazon SES connection at a time: once it is
connected, Amazon SES no longer appears in the list of connectors to add.
To change the route, disconnect it and connect again. Saving the same region,
From and To again replaces the stored key on the existing connection
instead of creating a duplicate, and sets it back to unverified until it
is checked again. Disconnecting a connection removes the stored key once no
other connection uses it.

#### What the access key needs

Bryn makes two SES calls with your key:

- `ses:GetSendQuota`, to check the connection.
- `ses:SendEmail`, to send a message.

Give the key a policy that allows those two actions and nothing else. A
dedicated IAM user for Bryn keeps it easy to rotate or revoke without
affecting anything else in your AWS account.

#### How Bryn verifies the connection

Right after you connect, Bryn reads your account's sending quota in the
region you entered. This is a read-only check: it sends no email. If AWS
accepts the key, the Bryn dashboard shows **Connection verified**. If not,
it shows **The connection could not be verified.** and you can correct the
details and check again.

The check confirms that your key works in that region. It does not
confirm that your From address is verified in SES, or that your account
is out of the SES sandbox. A connection can show as verified and still
have its sends rejected by SES until both are in place.

### Output

When Bryn sends through an SES connection, the message is:

- **From** the From address on the connection.
- **To** the To address on the connection, and only that address.
- **Plain text**, with a subject line and a text body.

SES enforces its own rules on every send, so get these right in your AWS
account first:

- **Verified sender.** SES only sends from an email address or domain you
  have verified as an identity, in the same region you give Bryn. Verifying
  the whole domain lets you use any address on it.
- **Sandbox.** New SES accounts start in the sandbox, where you can only
  send to verified addresses and at a low daily volume. Either verify the
  To address as well, or request production access so SES will deliver to
  any recipient.
- **Sending limits.** Your account's daily quota and per-second rate apply
  to everything you send through SES, Bryn included.

#### Set up the connection

**Verify your sender in SES**

In the SES console, pick the region you want to send from and create a
verified identity for your domain or From address. While your account
is in the sandbox, verify the To address too.

**Create an access key**

In IAM, create a user (or use an existing one) with a policy that
allows `ses:GetSendQuota` and `ses:SendEmail`, then create an access
key for it. Copy the secret access key now: AWS only shows it once.

**Connect in Bryn**

[Open the Amazon SES connect form](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?connect=ses)
in the Bryn dashboard and fill in the access key ID, secret access key,
region, From address and To address. If you already have an SES
connection, the link opens **Integrations** without the form.

**Check the result**

Bryn checks the key as soon as you connect. Once the dashboard shows
**Connection verified**, the connection is ready.

**You'll know it worked when** the connection is listed under
**Integrations** with your From address, To address and region, and shows
as verified. If verification fails, check that the access key is active,
that its policy allows `ses:GetSendQuota`, and that the region matches the
one your identity is verified in.

### Amazon SES documentation

- [What is Amazon SES?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html)
- [Setting up Amazon SES](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/setting-up.html)
- [Creating and verifying identities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/creating-identities.html)
- [Request production access (moving out of the sandbox)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/request-production-access.html)
- [Managing your sending quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/manage-sending-quotas.html)
- [Controlling access to Amazon SES with IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/control-user-access.html)
- [Managing access keys for IAM users](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html)
- [Amazon SES endpoints and regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/ses.html)

### Going further

- How Plays decide what to deliver and where: [Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays).
- Other destinations and how to keep alerts quiet: [Connect Slack and other outputs](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/outputs).

## Apify

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/apify

Apify is a platform for running web scrapers and automations, called actors,
in the cloud. Bryn uses your Apify account in two modes:

- **Enrichment**: Bryn runs a contact scraper over each account's website and
  stores the company's social profiles, published role mailboxes and phone
  numbers.
- **Input**: any actor or saved task you run in Apify (job boards, review
  sites, directory listings, page monitors) sends its results to Bryn when a
  run succeeds, one event per result.

### How Bryn integrates Apify

You connect Apify once, with your own Apify API token, under **Integrations**
in the Bryn dashboard. You find the token in Apify Console under
**Settings**, then **API & Integrations**. That one connection serves both
modes: Bryn uses it to start enrichment runs, and to read the results of the
runs your Input sources report.

- **Your account, your credits.** Apify bills compute and actor usage to the
  account that owns the token, so there is no shared Civic key. Every run Bryn
  starts, and every run you schedule, uses your Apify credits.
- **Verified without spending anything.** When you connect, Bryn checks the
  token by reading your Apify user profile. That starts no actor and costs
  nothing. A token Apify rejects is reported straight away.
- **A rejected token stops work.** If Apify later rejects the token, Bryn marks
  the connection as failed and stops using it until you reconnect.

### Enrichment

Bryn runs the Apify Store actor
[Contact Details Scraper](https://apify.com/vdrmota/contact-info-scraper) over
an account's website. It is an account-level lookup: it needs the account's
domain, and it never looks up individual people.

**What Bryn reads.** The scraper crawls the homepage and the pages one link
away (about, contact, team and similar), up to 10 pages. From what it finds,
Bryn keeps:

| Fact | What Bryn keeps |
|---|---|
| Social profiles | The company's own profile on LinkedIn (a company page), X, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. Personal profiles and share links are ignored. |
| Email addresses | Up to three role mailboxes such as `info@`, `sales@` or `support@`, on the account's own domain. Addresses with a person's name in them are never stored. |
| Phone numbers | Up to three numbers the site links as phone links. |

**When it runs.** Switch Apify on under **Configuration**, then
**Enrichment**. From then on, each account with a domain gets one Apify pass
when Bryn enriches it, and at most one every 30 days after that.

**What it costs.** Each run is capped at 10 pages, a short time limit and a
hard spending ceiling, so a typical pass costs a few cents of Apify credit. See
the actor's page in the Apify Store for its current pricing. If a slow site
hits the time limit, Bryn still keeps what the scraper found on the pages it
finished. A site that serves nothing in time is not retried until the next
pass, so it does not keep costing you runs.

**Where results appear.** On the account's company view, the values show
under **Company details** as links (a profile, an email or a phone number),
marked as coming from Apify. **Enrichment sources** lists which facts Apify
filled.

If your Apify account runs out of credits, Bryn retries the pass within the
hour. Top up or raise your usage limit in Apify and enrichment resumes on its
own.

### Input

An Apify Input source turns every succeeded run of one actor or saved task
into events in Bryn. Apify's run webhook says which run finished but does not
carry its results, so Bryn reads the results itself with your Apify
connection.

**What arrives.** Each result (each item in the run's dataset) becomes one
`item` event under the source's name, for example `apify.item`, with the
result's fields stored exactly as Apify Console shows them. Bryn reads up to
100 results per run and skips any single result over 32 KB. Failed, aborted
and timed out runs add nothing.

**How it stays safe.** Bryn only takes the run's ID from the webhook. It then
asks Apify for that run, confirms it succeeded and reads that run's own
results, so nobody can point Bryn at someone else's data. Apify retries a
failed delivery for about two days; Bryn skips results it has already stored,
so a retry never creates duplicates.

**How results map to accounts.** Every actor returns its own fields, so you
choose which field holds the company's website. A new source matches on a
`domain` field, which Contact Details Scraper returns. For other actors,
change it under account matching on the source, for example to
`companyWebsite` on a jobs actor. Matching only finds accounts Bryn already
has; it never creates one.

**How results become signals.** Results arrive straight away but raise
nothing until you map them. Map the source's `item` event to a signal under
**Configuration**, optionally with a condition on any field the actor returns.
See [signal mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).

#### Set up an Apify source

**Connect Apify first**

Add your API token under **Integrations** as described above. Without the
connection, Bryn cannot read run results and the source stores nothing.

**Add the source in Bryn**

Under **Integrations**, add an Apify input. Use one source per actor or
task, so each one's fields can be matched on their own. Bryn shows you an
endpoint URL and a secret.

**Add a webhook in Apify Console**

Open the actor or saved task, go to **Integrations** and add an HTTP
webhook. Choose **Run succeeded** as the event type and paste the endpoint
URL into **URL**.

**Add the secret as a header**

In **Headers template**, add the value Bryn shows you as JSON:
`{"Authorization": "Bearer <your source secret>"}`. Copy the full value
Bryn shows, including `Bearer`. Apify does not sign its
webhooks, so this header is how Bryn knows the call is yours.

**Keep the default payload and save**

Leave **Payload template** as it is. Bryn reads the run from Apify's
default payload.

**Point matching and mapping at the actor's fields**

On the source, set account matching to the field holding the company's
website, then map `item` events to a signal.

To run it regularly, use [Apify Schedules](https://docs.apify.com/platform/schedules).
A scheduled actor or task calls the source after every run, so there is
nothing to schedule in Bryn.

**You'll know it worked when** the next succeeded run's results appear as
`item` events on the source, attached to the matching accounts. If nothing
arrives, check that the header holds the full value Bryn showed you and that
the Apify connection is verified. If events arrive but match no account, the
matching field names something the actor does not return; results stored
before you fix it stay unmatched.

### Apify documentation

- [API and integrations (API token)](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/api)
- [Console settings](https://docs.apify.com/platform/console/settings)
- [Actors](https://docs.apify.com/platform/actors) and [saved tasks](https://docs.apify.com/platform/actors/running/tasks)
- [Webhooks](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/webhooks) and [webhook actions and payload template](https://docs.apify.com/platform/integrations/webhooks/actions)
- [Datasets](https://docs.apify.com/platform/storage/dataset)
- [Schedules](https://docs.apify.com/platform/schedules)
- [Contact Details Scraper](https://apify.com/vdrmota/contact-info-scraper)

### Going further

- Turn events into signals: [Signal mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).
- See how enrichment feeds scoring: [ICP and scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring).
- Act on signals: [Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays).
- All connectors: [Connectors](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors).

## Apollo

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/apollo

Apollo is a sales intelligence and engagement platform: a B2B contact and
company database with built-in email sequences. Bryn works with Apollo in
two modes on one API key: **Enrichment**, where Bryn looks up the
companies and people it sees, and **Output**, where a
[Play](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays) enrols a person into one of your Apollo sequences.

Bryn uses your own Apollo account, so every lookup and every enrolment
runs on your Apollo credits and plan.

### How Bryn integrates Apollo

You connect Apollo with an API key under **Integrations** in the Bryn
dashboard. One connection serves both modes: the enricher reads person
and account facts with the key, and Plays use the same key to add people
to sequences.

**The kind of API key decides what Bryn can do.** A standard Apollo API
key works for enrichment only. To enrol contacts into sequences, Bryn
needs a **master API key**, or a key scoped to sequences, email accounts
and contacts. If you connect a standard key, enrichment works, but Plays
cannot add anyone to a sequence until you reconnect with a key that has
that access.

When you enter the key, Bryn checks it straight away:

- **A rejected key** shows an error beside the field and you cannot
  connect it.
- **A key without sequence access** shows a note that it still works for
  enrichment. You can connect it for enrichment on its own.
- **A key with sequence access** loads your Apollo sequences and the
  mailboxes you can send from, so you can pick the connection's defaults.

Verifying the connection uses Apollo's account health check, which spends
no credits. Bryn keeps the key in encrypted storage; it is never shown
again, logged, or passed to Plays.

The default sequence and sending mailbox are stored on the connection.
To change them, reconnect Apollo, which checks the key again and offers
both pickers.

### Enrichment

Bryn looks Apollo up at two levels, each shown as its own source in the
Bryn dashboard:

- **Account level (Apollo)**: Bryn looks the company up by its domain and
  only keeps the record when Apollo's primary domain for it matches. It
  reads the company name, description, industry, employee count, annual
  revenue, total funding, founding year, country and location, number of
  retail locations, website, logo, and LinkedIn, X (Twitter) and Facebook
  URLs. Employee count, revenue, funding, country, industry and website
  feed the account's main fields, including its size band, which
  [scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring) uses.
- **Person level (Apollo (people))**: Bryn matches one person per lookup,
  using the strongest key it has: a LinkedIn profile URL first, then an
  email address, then a first and last name together with the company's
  domain. A first name alone is never sent, so Apollo cannot match a
  namesake. Bryn reads job title, first and last name, seniority (for
  example `VP` or `Director`), job function, LinkedIn URL, phone number,
  email address and its Apollo status, and employer.

Enrichment only fills gaps. Person details from Apollo fill empty fields
and never replace what a form, your team or a higher-priority source
already set. Bryn only takes an email address from Apollo when Apollo
marks it as verified and the person has none yet; guessed addresses, and
the placeholder Apollo returns when your plan cannot reveal an email, are
never stored as the person's email.

**When it runs.** Bryn looks an account up as soon as it has a domain,
and a person as soon as one of the keys above is known. A person with only
a name waits until the company domain arrives. Results are reused for 30
days before Bryn asks Apollo again.

**When Apollo refuses.** If Apollo rejects the key, Bryn flags the
connection so you can fix it under **Integrations**. If your plan does not
include an endpoint or you run out of credits, Bryn retries within the
hour, so accounts are filled in once you fix the plan.

### Output

A Play can add the person it acts on to an Apollo sequence. Apollo
enrols contacts, so each delivery happens in two steps:

1. Bryn creates the person as an Apollo contact, or finds the existing
   one. Apollo's duplicate check means a repeat delivery never creates a
   second contact or overwrites the one your team already has.
2. Bryn adds that contact to the sequence, sending from the chosen
   mailbox.

Bryn sends the person's email address (required, since sequences email
the contact), and where known their first and last name, job title,
company name, company website and LinkedIn URL.

#### Set it up

**Create a master API key in Apollo**

In Apollo's API settings, create a new key and turn on **Set as
master key**, or give it access to the sequences, email accounts and
contacts endpoints. Make sure the Apollo account has at least one
active mailbox and one sequence.

**Connect Apollo in the Bryn dashboard**

Go to **Integrations**, choose **Apollo** and paste the key. Pick a
**Default sequence** (optional) and the mailbox to **Send from**.
Apollo's own default mailbox is preselected.

**Add Apollo to a Play**

In the Play's outputs, add Apollo and pick the connection. Leave the
sequence and mailbox empty to use the connection's defaults, or pick
others for this Play. Turn on **Include unverified emails** only if
you want Apollo to enrol people whose email it has not verified;
Apollo skips them by default to protect your sending reputation.

**Test the entry**

Click **Test** on the Apollo entry. Bryn checks that the sequence
still exists and the mailbox is active, without enrolling anyone. If
the key cannot reach sequences, the test says so and asks for a
master key.

A connection only counts as an Apollo destination once it is verified and
has a sending mailbox. A connection made with a standard key is
enrichment only, and Plays cannot deliver to it.

**You'll know it worked when** the person appears as a contact in your
Apollo sequence, sending from the mailbox you picked. A person who is
already in that sequence counts as delivered, and is not added twice.

Apollo can also decline a person, for example because they are active in
another sequence or have no verified email. Bryn records that as a
skipped delivery with Apollo's reason, not as a failure. If the mailbox
has since been deactivated in Apollo, the delivery fails; link an active
mailbox in Apollo, then reconnect or pick it in the Play.

### Apollo documentation

- [Create an API key](https://docs.apollo.io/docs/create-api-key), including master keys and scoped keys
- [Authentication](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/authentication)
- [People enrichment](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/people-enrichment)
- [Organization enrichment](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/organization-enrichment)
- [Search for sequences](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/search-for-sequences)
- [Add contacts to a sequence](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/add-contacts-to-sequence)
- [Get a list of email accounts](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/get-a-list-of-email-accounts)
- [Rate limits](https://docs.apollo.io/reference/rate-limits)

### Going further

- Build the Play that enrols people: [Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays).
- See how enrichment feeds fit and scoring: [ICP and scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring).
- Compare with other connectors: [Connectors](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors).

## Calendly

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/calendly

Calendly is a scheduling tool: people pick a slot on one of your event
types and the meeting lands in your calendar. When someone books or
cancels, Calendly tells Bryn, and Bryn records it as a signal on that
person and their company.

Calendly works with Bryn in one mode: **Input**.

### How Bryn integrates Calendly

Calendly sends events to Bryn through a Calendly webhook subscription.
You set it up under [**Integrations**](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations)
in the Bryn dashboard, where adding Calendly creates a Calendly source in
your [Inputs](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?view=inputs) with its
own endpoint URL and signing secret.

Calendly has no screen for creating webhooks; a subscription can only be
created through its API with a personal access token. Bryn makes that call
for you if you paste a token (quick setup), or you can make it yourself
(manual setup). Either way, keep these in mind:

- **Webhooks need a paid Calendly plan.** The account the subscription is
  created for must be on the Standard, Teams or Enterprise plan.
- **Use an owner or admin token for everyone's bookings.** A token from an
  owner or admin of your Calendly organization can create an
  organization-wide subscription. A team member's token can only cover
  that member's own bookings.
- **Scopes.** Give the token `users:read`, `webhooks:read` and
  `webhooks:write`. (Manual setup only needs `users:read` and
  `webhooks:write`.)
- **Bryn doesn't keep your token.** Quick setup uses it for that one
  request and then discards it, so you can revoke it in Calendly straight
  after.

Every delivery is signed. Calendly signs each request with your source's
signing secret, and Bryn checks that signature before accepting anything.
A subscription created without the secret sends unsigned requests, and
Bryn refuses all of them.

### Input

#### What arrives

One subscription carries two Calendly events:

| Calendly event | Bryn signal | When |
|---|---|---|
| `invitee.created` | `meeting_booked` | Someone books a meeting with you |
| `invitee.canceled` | `meeting_canceled` | Someone cancels a meeting they booked |

A reschedule arrives from Calendly as a cancellation of the old slot plus
a new booking. Bryn treats it as a booking: the new slot raises
`meeting_booked`, and the cancellation half raises nothing, so a
rescheduled meeting never shows up as `meeting_canceled`.

#### How events match accounts and people

Calendly's booking events carry the invitee's details but no company, so
Bryn works from the invitee's email address:

- **Person**: the invitee is matched by email, and their name comes from
  the booking (the full name, plus first and last name when your event
  type asks for them separately).
- **Account**: the company is found from the email's domain, so a booking
  from `jane@acme.com` lands on Acme.
- **Personal addresses**: a booking from a free mail address (such as
  Gmail) still records the person, but can't place them at a company.

From there the signals behave like any other: they count towards the
account's [score](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring) and can trigger
[Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays). To change which signal an event raises, see
[Signal mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).

#### Connect Calendly

**Create a personal access token in Calendly**

On Calendly's [API and Webhooks page](https://calendly.com/integrations/api_webhooks)
(**Integrations**, then **API & Webhooks**), choose **Get a token
now** (or **Generate new token**) and give it the `users:read`,
`webhooks:read` and `webhooks:write` scopes. Create it as an owner or
admin if you want everyone's bookings.

**Add Calendly in the Bryn dashboard**

Go to [**Integrations**](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?view=inputs),
add **Calendly**, paste the token and click
**Connect Calendly**. Bryn checks the token first, so a mistyped token
or one missing `users:read` creates nothing.

**Check the scope Bryn reports**

Bryn creates the source and the Calendly subscription together. It
asks Calendly for an organization-wide subscription first, and if the
token's owner isn't an owner or admin, it falls back to that person's
own bookings. The finished screen tells you which one you got.

**Book a test meeting**

Book a slot on one of your own event types. The booking shows up in
Bryn within a few seconds.

If Calendly refuses the subscription after the source is created (most
often a plan without webhooks, or a missing scope), Bryn keeps the source
and shows you the reason, with quick setup ready to try again.

#### Set it up yourself

Choose **I'd rather set it up myself** when adding Calendly, or
**Set it up yourself** in the source's drawer. The dashboard shows the
steps with your endpoint URL and signing secret filled in:

1. Create a personal access token with the `users:read` and
   `webhooks:write` scopes.
2. Call `GET https://api.calendly.com/users/me` with the header
   `Authorization: Bearer <your token>`, and copy `current_organization`
   from the response.
3. Send `POST https://api.calendly.com/webhook_subscriptions` with the same
   header and a JSON body with:
   - `url`: your source's endpoint URL
   - `signing_key`: your source's signing secret
   - `events`: `["invitee.created", "invitee.canceled"]`
   - `organization`: your organization URI
   - `scope`: `"organization"` for everyone's bookings, or `"user"` for
     only yours (then also add `user`, your own user URI from the same
     lookup)
4. Book a test meeting and check it arrives.

Leave out `signing_key` and Calendly sends unsigned requests, which Bryn
refuses. Calendly cannot add a signing key to an existing subscription,
so you would need to delete it and create it again.

#### Keeping it working

- **Calendly gives up on a failing subscription.** If deliveries keep
  failing for 24 hours, Calendly disables the subscription and it has to
  be created again. If your test booking doesn't arrive, check the URL
  and the signing key.
- **Running quick setup again replaces the subscription.** Do this after
  you rotate the source's signing secret (the old subscription still signs
  with the old one) or after Calendly disables it. You'll need a fresh
  token, and the source must be turned on.
- **Both events share one subscription.** To receive only bookings or only
  cancellations, create the subscription yourself with just that event.
- **Deleting the source doesn't delete the Calendly subscription.** Bryn
  keeps no token, so it can't reach Calendly. Bryn refuses the
  subscription's deliveries from then on and Calendly disables it after a
  day, or you can delete it in Calendly yourself.
- **Organization subscriptions outlive their creator.** One created with
  an admin's token keeps working if that admin leaves your Calendly
  organization. A user-scoped one stops when its user leaves.

### Calendly documentation

- [Create a webhook subscription](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/api-guides/receive-data-from-scheduled-events-in-real-time-with-webhook-subscriptions):
  Calendly's guide, including organization and user scope
- [Personal access tokens](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/authentication/how-to-authenticate-with-personal-access-tokens)
  and [authorization scopes](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/authentication/scopes)
- [Find your organization or user URI](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/api-guides/how-to-find-the-organization-or-user-uri)
- [Create Webhook Subscription API reference](https://developer.calendly.com/api-docs/calendly-api/webhooks/create-webhook-subscription)
- [Webhook signatures](https://developer.calendly.com/api-docs/overview/webhooks/webhook-signatures)
  and [webhook errors and retries](https://developer.calendly.com/api-docs/overview/webhooks/webhook-errors)
- [Webhook payloads for rescheduled events](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/api-guides/see-how-webhook-payloads-change-when-invitees-reschedule-events)
- [Developer FAQ](https://developer.calendly.com/docs/getting-started/frequently-asked-questions),
  which lists the plans that include webhooks, and
  [Calendly pricing](https://calendly.com/pricing)

### Going further

- How events become signals: [Signal mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping)
- Act on a booking: [Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays)
- Other tools Bryn connects to: [Connectors](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors)

## Clay

Source: https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors/clay

Clay is a go-to-market data platform with a large database of companies
and people. Bryn uses Clay in one mode, **Enrichment**: when Bryn knows an
account's domain, it looks the company up in Clay and fills in its
firmographics (size, industry, type, country, location, revenue and
funding), which [scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring) and your
[Plays](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/plays) then use.

Clay is never a delivery destination. It does not appear in any Play's
outputs, and Bryn writes nothing to your Clay workspace.

### How Bryn integrates Clay

You connect Clay with a Clay API key under [**Integrations**](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations) in the
Bryn dashboard. The key is the only thing Bryn needs: there are no Clay tables,
columns or webhooks to set up, because Bryn calls Clay's company search
directly and reads the answer back in the same request.

**Lookups are billed to your Clay account.** Bryn uses the API key you
connect, and only that key, so every company lookup uses your Clay
workspace's credits. Bryn looks each account up at most once every 30
days to keep that spend predictable.

When you connect, Bryn checks the key by asking Clay who it belongs to.
That check is an identity read, not a search, so it costs nothing. The
connection only counts as verified once Clay accepts the key. Bryn keeps
the key in encrypted storage; it is never shown again, logged, or passed
to Plays.

The connect form also asks whether to **Use Clay for enrichment**. The
switch is on by default, and Bryn starts looking accounts up once the key
is verified. If you turn it off, the connection is saved but no lookups
run until you turn on **Clay enrichment** on the
[Clay card](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?connector=provider%3Aclay). To stop later, turn that switch off, or disconnect Clay
to remove the key altogether.

### Enrichment

Clay enrichment is **account level only**. Bryn asks Clay about the
company behind a domain; it never sends or requests anything about
individual people.

**What Bryn reads.** For a matched company, Bryn keeps the company name,
domain, description, company type, employee size band, country,
location, industry, annual revenue, total funding range, and LinkedIn
URL. Bryn puts these into the account's main fields:

- **Size, type and country** become the account's size band, company type
  and country, which [scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring) matches your ICP
  against.
- **Industry** comes from Clay as a LinkedIn industry name, which Bryn
  maps to its standard industry list, so it drives the industry part of
  your Fit score too. Because Clay's industries are more specific than
  most sources, Clay's industry wins when another source (such as your
  CRM or visitor identification) suggests a broader one. A few companies
  still carry an older LinkedIn industry name; Bryn maps those to the
  current one, and drops any it cannot map rather than guess.
- **Revenue and funding** are kept as Clay reports them, alongside the
  other Clay facts.

**Picking the right company.** A domain is often listed by companies that
do not own it: a business whose careers page runs on a hiring platform
lists that platform's domain, and a contractor may list a client's. So
Bryn does not trust Clay's first result. It asks for a few candidates and
only keeps a company whose own website is the domain Bryn asked about (or
the main site of that domain). When several remain, Bryn prefers the
exact match, then the company whose name matches the domain, then one
clearly larger than the rest. If none of these rules settles it, Bryn
keeps no answer rather than pick the wrong company.

When a lookup completes and Clay has no company Bryn will accept, Bryn
removes any earlier Clay answer for that account, so a wrong match does
not linger. When the result is ambiguous, the earlier answer stays as it
is.

**When it runs.** Bryn looks an account up in Clay when the account
produces a new [signal](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping), or when a mapped source
first creates the account. Accounts that existed before you turned Clay
on are enriched on their next signal, not all at once. An account without
a domain is skipped until a domain arrives, and then Clay runs straight
away.

Each account is looked up once per 30 days. A lookup that found nothing
also waits 30 days before Bryn asks again. A lookup that failed waits an
hour before Bryn retries.

**Where results appear.** Open an account in the Bryn dashboard: Clay is
listed under **Enrichment sources** with what it filled and when, and the
fields it filled show on the account. Enrichment activity from Clay is
also in the audit log, where you can filter by the Clay source.

**When Clay refuses.** If Clay rejects the key (for example because it
was revoked), Bryn marks the connection as needing attention on the
[Clay card](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?connector=provider%3Aclay);
reconnect with a working key to resume. If your Clay workspace runs out of credits, lookups fail and are retried later, so
accounts fill in once you top up. Clay rate limits and brief outages are
retried automatically.

#### Set it up

**Create a Clay API key**

In Clay, open your workspace settings, go to **API and CLI**, then
**API keys**, and create a key. Make sure the workspace has search
credits available.

**Connect Clay in the Bryn dashboard**

[Open the Clay connect form](https://bryn.civic.com/web/integrations?connect=clay) (or go to
**Integrations** and choose **Clay**), paste the key, leave **Use
Clay for enrichment** on, and connect. Bryn checks the key with Clay
before saving the connection.

**Check that it worked**

Wait for a new signal on an account that has a domain, then open the
account. Clay should be listed under **Enrichment sources**, with the
company's size, industry and country filled in.

### Clay documentation

- [Clay developer documentation](https://developers.clay.com/): overview
  of the Clay Public API that Bryn calls.
- [Authentication](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/authentication):
  how Clay API keys work and where to create one.
- [Searches](https://developers.clay.com/searches): the company search
  Bryn uses to look accounts up by domain.
- [Rate limits](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits): how
  Clay throttles API requests.
- [Credits](https://university.clay.com/docs/credits): how Clay bills
  usage against your workspace.

### Going further

- How accounts are scored against your ICP: [ICP and scoring](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/icp-and-scoring).
- How events become signals: [Signal mapping](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/signal-mapping).
- Every connector and the modes it supports: [Connectors](https://docs.civic.com/bryn/connectors).
